title: Jaya-Vijaya
body:
Jaya-Vijaya

Parikshith, having grasped the vastness of space and the endless cycles of time, asked the sage a deeper question: if all things move according to dharma, how is it that even those closest to the Lord may be cast into the world of birth and death? Shuka Maharishi answered that the ways of the divine cannot be understood by reason alone, for even the Lord's dearest may play their part in the unfolding of creation. To illustrate, he told the story of Jaya and Vijaya, the gatekeepers of Vaikuntham.
Here it should be understood that there are, in truth, two Vaikunthams, each an exact replica of the other. One is Sri Vaikuntham, the abode from which there is no return; the other is Karya Vaikuntham, to which gods and revered sages come in their times of need and from which they return once their purpose is served. It was at the gates of this Karya Vaikuntham, where the Lord Sriman Narayana rested upon His serpent recliner Adishesha, that Jaya and Vijaya stood guard — warriors unmatched and devotees unwavering.
One day the Four Kumaras — Sanaka, Sanandana, Sanatana, and Sanatkumara, the mindborn sons of Brahma — approached the gates seeking an audience with the Lord. Though ancient beyond measure, they bore the appearance of small children, for they had conquered time through their wisdom. Bound by their duty, Jaya and Vijaya barred the path, saying the Lord was in yoga-nidra and could not be disturbed. The sages, who had been welcomed even by the humblest of devotees, felt the weight of the refusal, and in their indignation they cursed the two guardians: for failing to see that the Lord belongs to all, they would be cast down from this realm of purity and made to walk the path of birth and death.
The words struck like thunder, for fear had never before existed in Vaikuntham. Jaya and Vijaya fell at the feet of the sages and begged forgiveness, but the curse could not be recalled. When the Lord Himself appeared, adorned in yellow silk and bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, He confirmed that the words of the great sages could not be undone. He offered His devoted gatekeepers a choice: they might be born seven times as His devotees and return to Him thereafter, or they might be born only three times as His adversaries, dying at His own hands each time before returning. Unwilling to bear so long a separation, Jaya and Vijaya chose the shorter path — three births as enemies of the Lord.
And so they fell. In their first birth they became Hiranyaksha and Hiranyakashipu, and the Lord descended as Varaha, the boar who lifted the Earth, and as Narasimha, who tore the tyrant apart to protect Prahlada. In their second birth they became Ravana and Kumbhakarna, and the Lord descended as Rama of Ayodhya to end their arrogance. In their final birth they became Shishupala and Dantavakra, and the Lord, now as Krishna, struck them down with the whirling Sudarshana Chakra. With that last blow the cycle was complete, and Jaya and Vijaya returned at last to their place at the gates of Vaikuntham. Thus, Shuka observed, even in opposition they were never truly apart from the Lord — for even the fiercest storm is but a whisper in the presence of the eternal.
